    "ruqyah_details.text.47": "The source reverses the rank clause in the Iblis narration. Muslim 2813b says the devil who creates the greatest fitnah is nearest to Iblis in rank; Urdu restores that wording. Muslim otherwise occurs only in the normalized English citation.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.52": "The source accidentally uses plural 'Prophets' when explaining who classed tiwalah as shirk; Urdu correctly attributes the statement to the Prophet. Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah occur only in the normalized English citation and are not duplicated in Urdu solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.54": "In Quran 7:119 the English inserts Pharaoh and his people, while the supplied Arabic retains an unspecified plural; Urdu follows the displayed verse. In Quran 10:81 the English paraphrases sayubtiluhu as exposing magic's worthlessness, while the Arabic directly says Allah will nullify it; Urdu preserves that direct meaning, consistent with reviewed parallels.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.56": "The severe-case symptom says the disoriented patient 'does know' where he is going, contradicting the surrounding description. Urdu corrects the evident missing negation and says he does not know where he is going.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.58": "The source incorrectly tells the reader to bring both arms near the face. Bukhari 5017 describes joining the palms, reciting, blowing into them and wiping the body; Urdu restores that action. Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud otherwise occur only in normalized English citations.",

"ruqyah_details.text.59": "The English translation of Quran 17:82 omits the final Arabic clause about the wrongdoers increasing only in loss; Urdu restores it, consistent with reviewed rows 41 and ruqyah_instants 163 and 274. The supplied Arabic ruqyah has a visible ╪┤╪▒┘â typo for ╪┤╪▒; Urdu follows the established wording confirmed by Muslim 2186, while preserving the frozen Arabic and Latin transliteration exactly.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.60": "Bukhari, Muslim and Ahmad occur only in normalized English citations and are not duplicated in Urdu solely for glossary matching. The stray trailing plus sign and quotation mark in the source are treated as editorial artifacts rather than content.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.61": "English glosses istihadha as continuous menstruation, but the following sentence correctly defines it as bleeding outside or following the normal menstrual period. Urdu uses the established term istihadha and explains it as bleeding outside normal menses.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.62": "English says to bring both arms near the face. The established Prophetic practice is to join the palms, recite, blow into them and wipe the body, so Urdu follows the same correction already documented for row 58.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.63": "Bukhari occurs only in the normalized English inline citation and is not duplicated in Urdu solely for glossary matching. The cited black-seed statement and Muslim wording are otherwise translated in full.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.66": "The Quran 7:119 English inserts Pharaoh and his people, and 10:81 paraphrases direct nullification; Urdu follows the supplied Arabic in both places, consistent with reviewed row 54. English also mistranslates al-Sami as All-Seeing; Urdu correctly says All-Hearing. 'Green lotus' is rendered by the established ruqyah ingredient, green sidr/lote leaves. Bukhari, Ibn Majah and Abu Dawud occur only in normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.67": "English misdescribes ghidha malikat al-nahl as honey produced by the queen bee; the ingredient is royal jelly, which Urdu names with the Arabic term and the familiar label. English also announces three types but lists four; Urdu introduces the supplied list without repeating the wrong count.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.68": "The symptom timing 'al-ast' is an evident typo for al-asr, matching the same symptom wording in row 62. Urdu correctly says the tightness begins around Asr.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.69": "The symptom timing 'al-ast' is an evident typo for al-asr, matching the same symptom wording in row 62. Urdu correctly says the tightness begins around Asr.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.71": "English mistranslates al-Sami as All-Seeing and ayn lammah as an accusing eye. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic with All-Hearing and a harmful evil eye. Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah occur only in normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.72": "English drops the first-person pronoun in 'because I have humiliated him' and the opening of the direct challenge 'I challenge you', and later misspells sahir as sanir. Urdu restores the evident intended speakers while translating all substantive content.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.73": "English repeatedly says pressed dates, but its own cited chapter identifies the established hadith wording as ajwah. Urdu correctly names seven ajwah dates. Bukhari occurs only in the normalized English citation and is not duplicated solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.75": "The exact Abu al-Darda congregational-prayer report is recorded at Abu Dawud 547 and Nasa'i 847, although the supplied inline citation names Bukhari and Muslim. Urdu follows the report's verified meaning while retaining the frozen normalized English citation; collection names are not duplicated solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.76": "The supplied paraphrase restricts the first report to missing qiyam al-layl until Fajr. Bukhari 3270 and Muslim 774 say the man slept until morning without rising for prayer, which Urdu preserves. Sa'id ibn Mansur is given rahimahullah rather than the source's Companion honorific. Abu Dawud occurs only in the retained normalized English citation.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.77": "The English anecdote incoherently has a jinn say that Allah gave 'us' a weapon to conquer 'them'. The surrounding speaker roles and the next clause identify the intended weapon as Prophetic invocations given to humans against jinn, which Urdu makes explicit. Bukhari and Muslim occur only in normalized English citations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.78": "English mistranslates Arabic nafthihi as the devil's voice. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic and the established reviewed parallel at dua row 192 with his spitting, while preserving the puffing and evil-suggestion clauses. The citation typos 'ai Ahmad' and 'Hadil' are normalized to Ahmad and Hadith without changing any reference number or markup. Collection names remain inside the normalized English citation.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.79": "Abu Dawud occurs only in the normalized English inline citation, which is retained under the project rules. Do not add an Urdu collection name solely to satisfy the canonical-term check.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.80": "English narrows supplied Arabic ahli/lahum to wife/her. Urdu follows the displayed plural wording as the household or family while retaining the marital context, consistent with reviewed dua row 394.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.81": "English says to recite during intercourse and corrupts Ibn Abbas's name. Bukhari 141 places the invocation before intercourse; Urdu restores that timing and the narrator's name, consistent with reviewed dua row 395.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.82": "English incorrectly attaches the Companion honorific RA to Allah. Bukhari 2311 says a guardian from Allah remains with the reciter until morning; Urdu preserves that meaning without the improper honorific.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.83": "English restricts the daily recitation to after Fajr and reduces the recorded good deeds and erased bad deeds to ten each. Muslim 2691 says one hundred recitations in a day, one hundred good deeds and one hundred bad deeds erased; Urdu follows the primary report.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.84": "Abu Dawud occurs only in the normalized English inline citation, which remains in English under the project rules. Do not add an Urdu collection name solely to satisfy the canonical-term check.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.85": "English renders Arabic al-Sami as All-Seeing. The supplied Arabic and Ibn Majah 3869 say All-Hearing; Urdu correctly uses ╪│╪¿ ┌⌐┌å┌╛ ╪│┘å┘å█Æ ┘ê╪º┘ä╪º.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.86": "Abu Dawud occurs only in the normalized English inline citation, which remains in English under the project rules. Do not add an Urdu collection name solely to satisfy the canonical-term check.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.87": "English prescribes the invocation morning and evening, but the cited Muslim 2709 report specifies three recitations in the evening. Urdu follows the cited primary wording.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.88": "The English paraphrase of Ibn al-Qayyim's arrow analogy is grammatically confused and internally contradictory. Urdu preserves its coherent meaning: the evil eye is likened to an arrow from the envier, which may strike an unprotected target, miss a defended one, or return to its source.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.89": "The isolated full stop between the listed Hasad and Nafs types is a source-layout artifact and is not reproduced as a separate Urdu paragraph.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.90": "English omits 'said' before the blessing instruction. Urdu restores the speaker and follows the established wording also preserved in Hisn al-Muslim 244. The Umm Salamah report in Bukhari 5739 says the girl was affected by the evil eye, not specifically by 'the eye of a jinn'; Urdu follows the primary report while retaining the surrounding source discussion as attributed claims.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.91": "The English translation of Quran 2:109 stops before the supplied Arabic clauses commanding pardon and affirming Allah's power; Urdu translates the complete displayed verse. English also inserts Muhammad and his followers into Quran 4:54, while the supplied Arabic says people generally; Urdu follows the Arabic without the explanatory insertion. Muhammad therefore occurs only in an omitted English gloss and is not inserted solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.92": "English incorrectly calls Nathara the Urdu term; Urdu uses the established term nazar-e-bad while retaining Ayn as the Arabic name. The English translation of Quran 68:51 is truncated, so Urdu translates the complete supplied Arabic. Arabic ayn lammah is rendered as a harmful eye rather than the source's narrower envious eye. Bukhari occurs only in the retained normalized English citation and is not duplicated solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.93": "Urdu renders all three Quranic passages directly and completely from the supplied Arabic, consistently with reviewed row 91, without importing explanatory names absent from the verses.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.94": "Bukhari and Tirmidhi occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. The supplied Bukhari 2033 citation does not contain the quoted mistakes-forgetfulness-coercion wording; Urdu translates that wording as supplied and verified at Ibn Majah 2043 while retaining the frozen citation for source-data audit. The jealousy-and-hatred report was checked against the matching wording at Musnad Ahmad 1412.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.95": "Hadith, Bukhari, Muslim and Ahmad occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated in Urdu solely for glossary matching. The source intentionally supplies the Sahl ibn Hunayf incident twice with small wording differences; Urdu preserves both complete versions rather than treating the second as accidental duplication.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.96": "Tirmidhi occurs only in the retained normalized English citation and is not duplicated solely for glossary matching. The source compresses the isnad into attribution to a freed slave of Az-Zubayr; Musnad Ahmad 1430-1432 has a freed slave of the family of Az-Zubayr reporting from Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, so Urdu restores Az-Zubayr as the Companion narrator.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.98": "Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi and Ahmad occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Al-Ayn and Al-Ilm are audio-track labels rather than untranslated English prose.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.99": "The source corrupts Qatadah and al-Suddi as Qaada and As-suday and contains a mechanically garbled explanation of Quran 12:68. Urdu restores the exegetes' names and the coherent stated explanation that the separate-gate precaution fulfilled Yaqub's concern about the evil eye, while preserving all displayed Arabic, verse numbers and citations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.100": "Bukhari, Muslim, Ibn Majah and Ahmad occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Urdu corrects the evident source typos Jabiri to Jabir, Al-Bukhati to Al-Bukhari, Ruga to Ruqya, and Sahin to Sahih without changing any reference number.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.101": "Bukhari and Muslim occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Urdu normalizes the corrupted Tafsir Ibn Kathir and An-Nihaya titles and restores the snake name al-Abtar, which the source mistranscribes as Albatross; the separate source footnote marker 2 is retained with both cited-note groups. In the later paragraph, the English incorrectly narrows Ibn al-Qayyim's general discussion of ways souls may exert influence into ways the evil eye is caused, producing the incoherent claim that protective prayers, ruqyah and refuge verses cause the evil eye; Urdu follows the Arabic text of Zad al-Ma'ad and describes forms of spiritual influence without making that claim.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.102": "The source misspells Sahl ibn Hunayf as Sahi and vaguely presents the Prophetic advice as being to Sahl. The verified incident has the Prophet addressing Amir ibn Rabi'a about Sahl and asking why he did not invoke blessing; Urdu restores both men and the speaker roles, consistent with the reviewed parallel in row 95 and Muwatta Malik 50:2.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.103": "Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur only in the retained normalized English citation and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. The English changes the primary wording 'left what was other than them' into discarding 'inappropriate' invocations; Urdu follows the cited Ibn Majah 3511 and matching Tirmidhi 2058 wording while preserving the frozen source reference number 2059. It also corrects the evident Al-Khudris and Jinr name typos; the Umm Salama wording agrees with Bukhari 5739.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.104": "The Bengali row 104 is unrelated and has different category/subcategory routing. For Sahl ibn Hunayf's washing, Urdu follows Muwatta Malik 50:2: hands, elbows, knees, ends of the feet and the inside of the lower garment, rather than the source's arms-and-legs wording; it also restores the command to invoke blessing and corrects the evident right-hand/right-foot error in the later washing instructions. The first ruqyah meaning follows the cited Muslim 2186 wording as 'every soul or envious eye' rather than treating the envier as a third separate object. The final healing supplication follows Bukhari 5743 and Muslim 2191a without the English source's unsupported first-person 'heal me'. All Arabic and transliteration remain frozen, and collection names remain only in normalized English citations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.106": "The English has a mechanical splice: 'A Raaqi is a p' is interrupted by the qualifications, while the continuation 'erson who...' appears after the numbered conditions. The Bengali row is unrelated and has different category/subcategory routing. Urdu repairs the broken word and incomplete opening, retains the supplied paragraph order, and renders every substantive definition and condition without importing the unrelated Bengali material.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.108": "The English incorrectly cites Quran 24:2 as a statement about punishing sorcerers. The verse is about the prescribed punishment for zina; Urdu translates the supplied excerpt accurately and explicitly identifies its real context rather than repeating the false attribution. The source's experiential claims about accepted prayers and returning sorcery harm are retained as the author's attributed views, not recast as universally established rulings.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.109": "This five-part source contains prescriptive and experiential claims about retaliating jinn, killing jinn in dreams, repeating Ayat al-Kursi eleven times, recurring sorcery, Quran-recited bath water and perfume attracting angels. Urdu preserves every substantive claim but explicitly attributes these claims and recommendations to the author rather than presenting them as established Quranic or Prophetic rulings. The evident corruption 'Do not stop until you are cured and once you continue' is rendered coherently as continuing treatment until recovery and then resuming ruqyah work. Quran 7:201 is translated directly and completely.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.110": "The final promise that Allah will send angels, Muslim jinn or decisive dreams in distress is retained as the author's stated expectation, not recast as a universally established promise. The quoted principle that Allah aids a servant while the servant aids his brother was checked against Abu Dawud 4946.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.111": "The source's phrase 'divine authorisation' and its proposed signs are presented explicitly as the author's wording and interpretation. Urdu renders it as perceived divine facilitation and permission, avoiding any implication of revelation while retaining the advice and all supplied signs.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.113": "The no-barrier principle for the prayer of an oppressed person agrees with Bukhari 2448. The further comparison with an ordinary Muslim's supplication and the author's claimed benefits are retained as his inferences and experience. The ten possible faults of a fee-charging raqi remain conditional possibilities rather than universal accusations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.116": "The Fajr wording and protection from every disliked thing and Satan agree with Tirmidhi 3474, while the Maghrib protection wording is found in Tirmidhi 3534; Urdu avoids overstating this as an absolute guarantee against every conceivable harm. The seven-Ajwa report agrees with Bukhari 5445 and Muslim 2047. The source's additional advice about when to eat Ajwa, taking it on an empty stomach after Fajr and waiting an hour is retained explicitly as the author's recommendation rather than inserted into the hadith.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.117": "The statement about the Prophet's heart is an interpretive paraphrase of Muslim 2702a, not its exact wording; Urdu distinguishes the author's explanation from the report while retaining Muslim 4:2075 as supplied.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.118": "The claim that sins weaken a raqi against jinn is retained as the author's view, not independently certified religious or clinical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.119": "The source's causal claims linking a patient's sins to jinn speech and disruptive behaviour are explicitly attributed to the author. Acceptance of Jibril's ruqyah was checked against Muslim 2186.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.120": "The proposed link between sins and violent or unusual behaviour, and the author's claimed obligation of physical intervention, remain attributed source views rather than universal rulings or clinical diagnoses. The translated video title retains part 3.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.122": "The Bengali same-ID row is unrelated. Al-Lalkai's original report 2278 identifies Sulayman ibn Umayyah as a descendant of Urwah ibn Masud, not an Ibn Masud transmitter, and concerns washing the departing woman's traces with water and sidr, not advising that woman to wash away magic. Urdu corrects the source's garbled chain/summary from the cited primary text. Both supplication meanings follow the frozen Arabic, compared with Bukhari 5743 and Muslim 2186, while Arabic and Roman transliterations remain verbatim. Bukhari and Muslim occur only in normalized English citations. Quran reference 46:29:32 is normalized to 46:29-32 without changing any number. Therapeutic claims and proposed recitation schedules remain attributed recommendations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.123": "Senna's blanket authenticity claim and the supplied grading statements remain explicitly attributed; Tirmidhi 2081 and 2048 carry differing Tirmidhi/Darussalam assessments. Ibn Majah 3457 confirms Abu Ubayy ibn Umm Haram, the two-qiblah description and the senna/sannut wording. The unexplained Umar ibn al-Khattab/Mustadrak reference is retained as a source attribution, not conflated with Asma's chain. The source's unusual mouth-inhalation explanation is attributed, not adopted as a definition of nasal drops. See the batch review for unresolved source and clinical issues.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.124": "The contradictory senna recipes, durations and medicinal claims are retained as attributed source material, not approved dosing. The claim of no side effects remains inside an attributed quotation. The awkward 'spread of hair' is rendered as hair shedding, matching the classical Arabic expression intishar al-shar in Zad al-Maad. All source quantities and numerals are preserved; clinical concerns are documented in the batch review.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.125": "The source's ingested-magic treatment, repeated-course interval and claimed diagnostic role of other therapies remain the author's recommendations. All cautions, including the original pregnancy/nursing prohibition, are retained without certifying them as current medical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.126": "The Palestinian-oil preference is presented as the author's inference, not part of Quran 24:35. The verse's supplied Arabic is preserved verbatim and its meaning translated completely. The oil hadith was checked against Tirmidhi 1851; Tirmidhi appears only in the normalized English citation.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.127": "The Ajwa narrator is Amir ibn Sad reporting from his father Sad ibn Abi Waqqas, as in Bukhari 5445 and Muslim 2047b; the garbled second Amr attribution and Companion honorific for the son are corrected. Broader claims about other dates, later treatment, and dates being indispensable to a balanced fruit diet remain attributed opinions. Sihr occurs only within a normalized English book citation and need not force an extra Urdu term into the prose.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.128": "Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Majah occur in normalized English citations. Ibn Majah 3449 is not Buraidah's report as the source claims, but the Khalid bin Sad/Ghalib/Aisha report; Urdu flags the attribution without silently changing the number. Other clinical claims remain attributed to the author.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.129": "Muslim occurs only in a normalized English citation in this four-part text. The original IslamQA argument and all cited numbers are preserved; no redundant Urdu collection name is inserted solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.131": "Bukhari and Muslim occur only in normalized English citations. The Umm Qays report was checked against Bukhari 5713. The separate Anas report in Bukhari 5696 refers to sea costus, which the source conflates with Indian costus. Historical medical claims are attributed, not certified.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.139": "Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur only in normalized English citations. The source labels the angel report Sahih despite disputed grading; Urdu notes this. The Bukhari 5371 cupping citation is false and is corrected to the relevant Bukhari 5696 text. The source's detoxification explanation is attributed rather than included in hadith wording.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.142": "Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi occur only in normalized English citations. Qaf 50:9 says blessed water, not a rule that rainwater must be used for ruqyah; the Palestinian oil preference and water-diluted honey are the author's or shaykh's inferences, not Quranic or hadith requirements. The hadith quotations and verse meanings were compared with their primary texts.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.149": "The English gloss of Quran 2:102 inserts Children of Israel as an explicit subject, but the supplied Arabic only says they. Urdu translates the supplied Arabic without that unsupported insertion. All eight split parts, Arabic verse blocks, numbers and recitation headings remain intact.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.154": "Bukhari and Muslim appear only in normalized English citations. The report about unacted and unspoken involuntary thoughts agrees with Bukhari 2528; Urdu preserves it without turning intrusive thoughts into moral guilt.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.155": "Muslim appears only in a normalized English citation. Abu Hurayra's first report agrees with Muslim 132a. The source's Muslim 2203 reference for Ibn Abbas and the charcoal/whispering report is unrelated; the report is Abu Dawud 5112, so Urdu corrects that citation and records the numeric change.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.156": "Arabic and Muslim 134b say belief in Allah and His messengers (plural), not the English singular Messenger. Abu Dawud 5110 supports First, Last, Evident and Immanent, not the source's Most High and Most Near. Arabic blocks and transliterations stay verbatim; the Urdu meanings follow the cited originals.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.158": "Ahmad 22211 records the Prophet's supplication in the third person (his sin, heart, chastity); the displayed source Arabic adapts it to the first person. English reverses the explanation. Urdu explains the adaptation correctly without altering Arabic or transliteration. Abu Dawud 1551 supports the second dua.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.159": "Reported nighttime assaults are not confirmed as caused by jinn; Urdu attributes that interpretation to the author and adds advice to obtain medical and assault support for injuries or suspected assault. The source's 11-times recitation is an author recommendation, not represented as Sunnah.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.160": "Psoriasis and eczema have medical causes. The author's claims about sihr, stopping prescribed medicines, vinegar on broken skin and a six-month herbal preparation are attributed, not endorsed; Urdu adds explicit advice to retain prescribed treatment and seek dermatology guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.161": "Stomach symptoms do not prove ingested sihr. The emetic, senna/rhubarb mixture and detox claims are presented as the author's views; Urdu retains the consultation warning and advises assessment for persistent symptoms.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.162": "The source's As-Sura 49-50 is Ash-Shura 42:49-50. Infertility is not evidence of sin or magic; Urdu attributes Hasan al-Basri's counsel rather than blaming a couple. Al-Baqarah ends at verse 286, so its erroneous 284-287 range is corrected to 284-286. Citation numbers are otherwise kept as supplied.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.163": "The narrator is Uthman ibn Abi al-As. The source's malformed HTML and Roman transliteration are preserved as supplied; Urdu meaning follows the displayed Arabic. Muslim 2202 gives a related variant; source Arabic is not silently replaced.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.166": "Bukhari and Tirmidhi occur only in normalized English citations in the five-part source; Urdu keeps them in citation form rather than adding redundant collection names. The cancer comparison is explicitly a metaphor, not medical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.169": "Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur in normalized English citations and are not duplicated in Urdu. The source's Bukhari 5371 is about a deceased debtor, not cupping; the relevant Bukhari 5696 names cupping and sea costus among the best treatments, so Urdu corrects both reference and the incomplete English gloss.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.176": "Bukhari and Muslim appear only in the retained normalized English citation. The source's supplement/heat/stasis interpretation is attributed to the author, not embedded in the hadith.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.195": "Bukhari appears only in the normalized English citation. Ibn Majah 3487 is graded weak by Darussalam on Sunnah.com; the source's Sahih label is not adopted as a verified grading."
  },
  "number_overrides": {
    "dua_infos.description.39": "The source's Abu Dawud 2131 is an unrelated marriage report (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:2131); the kindness-and-recompense narration is Abu Dawud 1672 (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1672). Nasa'i 587 is an unrelated prayer-time report and remains flagged rather than cited as corroboration.",
    "dua_infos.description.40": "The Ibn Umar traveler report is Bukhari 6416 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6416), not the source's 1283; the source's 21373 is garbled bibliographic OCR and has no reliable referent in this batch.",
    "dua_infos.description.42": "The source's 112 o'clock is OCR-corrupt and is rendered contextually as 1 or 2 o'clock. Muslim 2821 for the best night prayer is changed to matching Muslim 1163 (https://sunnah.com/muslim:1163b).",
    "dua_infos.description.2": "The Bengali source's Tirmidhi 2481 is unrelated to the quoted Fajr-to-sunrise hadith; the actual report is https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:586 . Compare https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2481 . Urdu changes 2481 to 586.",
    "dua_infos.description.7": "Bengali OCR splits Jami al-Ulum wa al-Hikam 1/269-275 as 1/2 69-275, and Musnad Ahmad 11133 as 111 33. Urdu joins the digits. Compare https://hadeethenc.com/en/browse/hadith/5100 and https://d1.islamhouse.com/data/ar/ih_books/single4/ar_Terms_of_prayer.pdf .",
    "dua_infos.description.8": "Corrections in parts 1-15: Nasa'i 1285 -> 1284 for the Fudalah report (https://sunnah.com/nasai:1284); OCR 1/2 69-275 -> 1/269-275; Buraidah's cited Nasa'i 1300 -> Abu Dawud 1493 (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1493); the Anas full-wording report al-Adab al-Mufrad 705 -> Nasa'i 1300 and the Mihjan report Nasa'i 1300 -> 1301 (https://sunnah.com/nasai:1300 and https://sunnah.com/nasai:1301); long rain report Bukhari 932 -> 933 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:933). Numeric multisets were separately audited part by part.",
    "dua_infos.description.9": "Part 2: source Bukhari 755 after the three-supplications report -> Abu Dawud 1536 and Tirmidhi 1905; Bukhari 755 remains correctly with the preceding Sa'd report. Muslim 1610 is added for the full Arwa story because Bukhari 2452 contains only the land-usurpation saying. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:755 , https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1536 , https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:1905 , https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2452 and https://sunnah.com/muslim:1610b .",
    "dua_infos.description.10": "Part 1: source Tirmidhi 2370 appears twice for different supplication reports; the quoted matns are Tirmidhi 3370 and 3373 respectively. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3370 and https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3373 . The source's numbering 1/2/3 in the three-outcomes report is preserved in Urdu.",
    "dua_infos.description.17": "Source Bukhari 7091 is unrelated to Ibn Umar's report about two praiseworthy forms of envy; Urdu uses Bukhari 5025 after checking https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5025 and https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7091 . Other numeric references are retained, including unresolved Indian-edition OCR 21123.",
    "dua_infos.description.18": "In part 2 the source's Abu Dawud 282 is unrelated to the quoted finger-counting narration; Urdu uses Abu Dawud 1502 (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1502). The complete Yusayrah wording is Tirmidhi 3583, not the second source citation to Tirmidhi 3486 (https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3583); the first 3486 citation for Abdullah ibn Amr stays (https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3486). Numeric multisets were separately audited part by part.",
    "dua_infos.description.19": "Bengali al-Zukhruf 1 -> Quran 43:87, the matching passage where they say Allah created them; checked https://quran.com/43:87 and compared https://quran.com/43:1 . All other numeric references in record 19 are preserved.",
    "dua_infos.description.20": "Part 6: source Bukhari 13445 -> 3445 for the quoted warning against exaggerating praise, checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3445 . All other part-wise numeric multisets were checked.",
    "dua_infos.description.23": "Source Abu Dawud 4683 -> 4681 (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4681), Abu Dawud 5127 -> 5126 for Abu Dharr (https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5126), and the final Muslim 2566 -> 2567 for the angel visiting a believer (https://sunnah.com/muslim:2567a). The earlier Muslim 2566 shade report remains (https://sunnah.com/muslim:2566). Other numeric references are preserved, including unresolved al-Silsilah 2/398-700.",
    "dua_infos.description.25": "Part 4: source Bukhari 1880 concerns the protection of Medina (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1880), not Abu Hurayrah's three recommendations. The matching fasting-book report is Bukhari 1981 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1981), so Urdu corrects only that number. All part-wise numeric multisets were separately checked.",
    "dua_infos.description.27": "Part 6: source Muslim 2654 -> 2655 for Allah turning hearts toward obedience. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2654 and https://sunnah.com/muslim:2655 . Other source numbers remain unchanged; the correction is limited to this citation.",
    "dua_infos.description.32": "Part 2 Bukhari 3993 -> 7430 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7430); part 6 Bukhari 213 -> 2312 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2312); part 10 Bukhari 1954 -> 2059 (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2059). The former numbers 3993 and 1954 are unrelated reports in modern numbering; all other numerals in 046-049 were checked part by part.",
    "dua_infos.description.33": "Part 3 source Muslim 275 -> 2735 for the impatient-supplication hadith (https://sunnah.com/muslim:2735c). In part 7, source Bukhari 2585 -> 2736 for the 99-names report (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2736); the former modern number is about gifts (https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2585). All other numeric values in 049-055 were checked part by part and retained.",
    "ruqyah_instants.translation.184": "English is an unrelated duplicate numbered Quran 27:73-75, while the supplied Arabic, title and Bengali are Quran 33:70-71. Urdu preserves the actual verse numbers 70-71.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.45": "The source calls Surah al-Jinn chapter 62, but it is Quran chapter 72. Urdu corrects the chapter number while retaining the frozen source.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.83": "English gives ten good deeds and ten bad deeds erased, while Muslim 2691 explicitly gives one hundred of each. Urdu preserves the primary report's numbers.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.139": "The supplied Bukhari 5371 citation is unrelated to cupping. The relevant report on the best treatments, including cupping and sea costus, is Bukhari 5696; Urdu corrects that number and wording after checking https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5696 and https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5371 .",
    "ruqyah_details.text.155": "The source cites Muslim 2203 for Ibn Abbas's charcoal/whispering report, but Muslim 2203 concerns the devil's interference with prayer. The quoted Ibn Abbas wording is Abu Dawud 5112; Urdu corrects the reference after checking https://sunnah.com/muslim:2203 and https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5112 .",
    "ruqyah_details.text.162": "Al-Baqarah ends at 286, so the source's 284-287 is impossible and Urdu correctly gives 284-286; checked https://quran.com/2/286 .",
    "ruqyah_details.text.169": "The cited Bukhari 5371 concerns a deceased debtor, not cupping. Urdu corrects this to the relevant Bukhari 5696; checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5371 and https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5696 ."
  },
