    "ruqyah_details.text.96": "Tirmidhi occurs only in the retained normalized English citation and is not duplicated solely for glossary matching. The source compresses the isnad into attribution to a freed slave of Az-Zubayr; Musnad Ahmad 1430-1432 has a freed slave of the family of Az-Zubayr reporting from Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, so Urdu restores Az-Zubayr as the Companion narrator.",

"ruqyah_details.text.98": "Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi and Ahmad occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Al-Ayn and Al-Ilm are audio-track labels rather than untranslated English prose.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.99": "The source corrupts Qatadah and al-Suddi as Qaada and As-suday and contains a mechanically garbled explanation of Quran 12:68. Urdu restores the exegetes' names and the coherent stated explanation that the separate-gate precaution fulfilled Yaqub's concern about the evil eye, while preserving all displayed Arabic, verse numbers and citations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.100": "Bukhari, Muslim, Ibn Majah and Ahmad occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Urdu corrects the evident source typos Jabiri to Jabir, Al-Bukhati to Al-Bukhari, Ruga to Ruqya, and Sahin to Sahih without changing any reference number.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.101": "Bukhari and Muslim occur only in retained normalized English citations and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. Urdu normalizes the corrupted Tafsir Ibn Kathir and An-Nihaya titles and restores the snake name al-Abtar, which the source mistranscribes as Albatross; the separate source footnote marker 2 is retained with both cited-note groups. In the later paragraph, the English incorrectly narrows Ibn al-Qayyim's general discussion of ways souls may exert influence into ways the evil eye is caused, producing the incoherent claim that protective prayers, ruqyah and refuge verses cause the evil eye; Urdu follows the Arabic text of Zad al-Ma'ad and describes forms of spiritual influence without making that claim.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.102": "The source misspells Sahl ibn Hunayf as Sahi and vaguely presents the Prophetic advice as being to Sahl. The verified incident has the Prophet addressing Amir ibn Rabi'a about Sahl and asking why he did not invoke blessing; Urdu restores both men and the speaker roles, consistent with the reviewed parallel in row 95 and Muwatta Malik 50:2.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.103": "Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur only in the retained normalized English citation and are not duplicated solely for glossary matching. The English changes the primary wording 'left what was other than them' into discarding 'inappropriate' invocations; Urdu follows the cited Ibn Majah 3511 and matching Tirmidhi 2058 wording while preserving the frozen source reference number 2059. It also corrects the evident Al-Khudris and Jinr name typos; the Umm Salama wording agrees with Bukhari 5739.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.104": "The Bengali row 104 is unrelated and has different category/subcategory routing. For Sahl ibn Hunayf's washing, Urdu follows Muwatta Malik 50:2: hands, elbows, knees, ends of the feet and the inside of the lower garment, rather than the source's arms-and-legs wording; it also restores the command to invoke blessing and corrects the evident right-hand/right-foot error in the later washing instructions. The first ruqyah meaning follows the cited Muslim 2186 wording as 'every soul or envious eye' rather than treating the envier as a third separate object. The final healing supplication follows Bukhari 5743 and Muslim 2191a without the English source's unsupported first-person 'heal me'. All Arabic and transliteration remain frozen, and collection names remain only in normalized English citations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.106": "The English has a mechanical splice: 'A Raaqi is a p' is interrupted by the qualifications, while the continuation 'erson who...' appears after the numbered conditions. The Bengali row is unrelated and has different category/subcategory routing. Urdu repairs the broken word and incomplete opening, retains the supplied paragraph order, and renders every substantive definition and condition without importing the unrelated Bengali material.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.108": "The English incorrectly cites Quran 24:2 as a statement about punishing sorcerers. The verse is about the prescribed punishment for zina; Urdu translates the supplied excerpt accurately and explicitly identifies its real context rather than repeating the false attribution. The source's experiential claims about accepted prayers and returning sorcery harm are retained as the author's attributed views, not recast as universally established rulings.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.109": "This five-part source contains prescriptive and experiential claims about retaliating jinn, killing jinn in dreams, repeating Ayat al-Kursi eleven times, recurring sorcery, Quran-recited bath water and perfume attracting angels. Urdu preserves every substantive claim but explicitly attributes these claims and recommendations to the author rather than presenting them as established Quranic or Prophetic rulings. The evident corruption 'Do not stop until you are cured and once you continue' is rendered coherently as continuing treatment until recovery and then resuming ruqyah work. Quran 7:201 is translated directly and completely.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.110": "The final promise that Allah will send angels, Muslim jinn or decisive dreams in distress is retained as the author's stated expectation, not recast as a universally established promise. The quoted principle that Allah aids a servant while the servant aids his brother was checked against Abu Dawud 4946.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.111": "The source's phrase 'divine authorisation' and its proposed signs are presented explicitly as the author's wording and interpretation. Urdu renders it as perceived divine facilitation and permission, avoiding any implication of revelation while retaining the advice and all supplied signs.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.113": "The no-barrier principle for the prayer of an oppressed person agrees with Bukhari 2448. The further comparison with an ordinary Muslim's supplication and the author's claimed benefits are retained as his inferences and experience. The ten possible faults of a fee-charging raqi remain conditional possibilities rather than universal accusations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.116": "The Fajr wording and protection from every disliked thing and Satan agree with Tirmidhi 3474, while the Maghrib protection wording is found in Tirmidhi 3534; Urdu avoids overstating this as an absolute guarantee against every conceivable harm. The seven-Ajwa report agrees with Bukhari 5445 and Muslim 2047. The source's additional advice about when to eat Ajwa, taking it on an empty stomach after Fajr and waiting an hour is retained explicitly as the author's recommendation rather than inserted into the hadith.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.117": "The statement about the Prophet's heart is an interpretive paraphrase of Muslim 2702a, not its exact wording; Urdu distinguishes the author's explanation from the report while retaining Muslim 4:2075 as supplied.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.118": "The claim that sins weaken a raqi against jinn is retained as the author's view, not independently certified religious or clinical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.119": "The source's causal claims linking a patient's sins to jinn speech and disruptive behaviour are explicitly attributed to the author. Acceptance of Jibril's ruqyah was checked against Muslim 2186.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.120": "The proposed link between sins and violent or unusual behaviour, and the author's claimed obligation of physical intervention, remain attributed source views rather than universal rulings or clinical diagnoses. The translated video title retains part 3.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.122": "The Bengali same-ID row is unrelated. Al-Lalkai's original report 2278 identifies Sulayman ibn Umayyah as a descendant of Urwah ibn Masud, not an Ibn Masud transmitter, and concerns washing the departing woman's traces with water and sidr, not advising that woman to wash away magic. Urdu corrects the source's garbled chain/summary from the cited primary text. Both supplication meanings follow the frozen Arabic, compared with Bukhari 5743 and Muslim 2186, while Arabic and Roman transliterations remain verbatim. Bukhari and Muslim occur only in normalized English citations. Quran reference 46:29:32 is normalized to 46:29-32 without changing any number. Therapeutic claims and proposed recitation schedules remain attributed recommendations.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.123": "Senna's blanket authenticity claim and the supplied grading statements remain explicitly attributed; Tirmidhi 2081 and 2048 carry differing Tirmidhi/Darussalam assessments. Ibn Majah 3457 confirms Abu Ubayy ibn Umm Haram, the two-qiblah description and the senna/sannut wording. The unexplained Umar ibn al-Khattab/Mustadrak reference is retained as a source attribution, not conflated with Asma's chain. The source's unusual mouth-inhalation explanation is attributed, not adopted as a definition of nasal drops. See the batch review for unresolved source and clinical issues.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.124": "The contradictory senna recipes, durations and medicinal claims are retained as attributed source material, not approved dosing. The claim of no side effects remains inside an attributed quotation. The awkward 'spread of hair' is rendered as hair shedding, matching the classical Arabic expression intishar al-shar in Zad al-Maad. All source quantities and numerals are preserved; clinical concerns are documented in the batch review.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.125": "The source's ingested-magic treatment, repeated-course interval and claimed diagnostic role of other therapies remain the author's recommendations. All cautions, including the original pregnancy/nursing prohibition, are retained without certifying them as current medical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.126": "The Palestinian-oil preference is presented as the author's inference, not part of Quran 24:35. The verse's supplied Arabic is preserved verbatim and its meaning translated completely. The oil hadith was checked against Tirmidhi 1851; Tirmidhi appears only in the normalized English citation.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.127": "The Ajwa narrator is Amir ibn Sad reporting from his father Sad ibn Abi Waqqas, as in Bukhari 5445 and Muslim 2047b; the garbled second Amr attribution and Companion honorific for the son are corrected. Broader claims about other dates, later treatment, and dates being indispensable to a balanced fruit diet remain attributed opinions. Sihr occurs only within a normalized English book citation and need not force an extra Urdu term into the prose.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.128": "Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Majah occur in normalized English citations. Ibn Majah 3449 is not Buraidah's report as the source claims, but the Khalid bin Sad/Ghalib/Aisha report; Urdu flags the attribution without silently changing the number. Other clinical claims remain attributed to the author.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.129": "Muslim occurs only in a normalized English citation in this four-part text. The original IslamQA argument and all cited numbers are preserved; no redundant Urdu collection name is inserted solely for glossary matching.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.131": "Bukhari and Muslim occur only in normalized English citations. The Umm Qays report was checked against Bukhari 5713. The separate Anas report in Bukhari 5696 refers to sea costus, which the source conflates with Indian costus. Historical medical claims are attributed, not certified.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.139": "Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur only in normalized English citations. The source labels the angel report Sahih despite disputed grading; Urdu notes this. The Bukhari 5371 cupping citation is false and is corrected to the relevant Bukhari 5696 text. The source's detoxification explanation is attributed rather than included in hadith wording.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.142": "Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi occur only in normalized English citations. Qaf 50:9 says blessed water, not a rule that rainwater must be used for ruqyah; the Palestinian oil preference and water-diluted honey are the author's or shaykh's inferences, not Quranic or hadith requirements. The hadith quotations and verse meanings were compared with their primary texts.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.149": "The English gloss of Quran 2:102 inserts Children of Israel as an explicit subject, but the supplied Arabic only says they. Urdu translates the supplied Arabic without that unsupported insertion. All eight split parts, Arabic verse blocks, numbers and recitation headings remain intact.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.154": "Bukhari and Muslim appear only in normalized English citations. The report about unacted and unspoken involuntary thoughts agrees with Bukhari 2528; Urdu preserves it without turning intrusive thoughts into moral guilt.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.155": "Muslim appears only in a normalized English citation. Abu Hurayra's first report agrees with Muslim 132a. The source's Muslim 2203 reference for Ibn Abbas and the charcoal/whispering report is unrelated; the report is Abu Dawud 5112, so Urdu corrects that citation and records the numeric change.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.156": "Arabic and Muslim 134b say belief in Allah and His messengers (plural), not the English singular Messenger. Abu Dawud 5110 supports First, Last, Evident and Immanent, not the source's Most High and Most Near. Arabic blocks and transliterations stay verbatim; the Urdu meanings follow the cited originals.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.158": "Ahmad 22211 records the Prophet's supplication in the third person (his sin, heart, chastity); the displayed source Arabic adapts it to the first person. English reverses the explanation. Urdu explains the adaptation correctly without altering Arabic or transliteration. Abu Dawud 1551 supports the second dua.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.159": "Reported nighttime assaults are not confirmed as caused by jinn; Urdu attributes that interpretation to the author and adds advice to obtain medical and assault support for injuries or suspected assault. The source's 11-times recitation is an author recommendation, not represented as Sunnah.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.160": "Psoriasis and eczema have medical causes. The author's claims about sihr, stopping prescribed medicines, vinegar on broken skin and a six-month herbal preparation are attributed, not endorsed; Urdu adds explicit advice to retain prescribed treatment and seek dermatology guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.161": "Stomach symptoms do not prove ingested sihr. The emetic, senna/rhubarb mixture and detox claims are presented as the author's views; Urdu retains the consultation warning and advises assessment for persistent symptoms.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.162": "The source's As-Sura 49-50 is Ash-Shura 42:49-50. Infertility is not evidence of sin or magic; Urdu attributes Hasan al-Basri's counsel rather than blaming a couple. Al-Baqarah ends at verse 286, so its erroneous 284-287 range is corrected to 284-286. Citation numbers are otherwise kept as supplied.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.163": "The narrator is Uthman ibn Abi al-As. The source's malformed HTML and Roman transliteration are preserved as supplied; Urdu meaning follows the displayed Arabic. Muslim 2202 gives a related variant; source Arabic is not silently replaced.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.166": "Bukhari and Tirmidhi occur only in normalized English citations in the five-part source; Urdu keeps them in citation form rather than adding redundant collection names. The cancer comparison is explicitly a metaphor, not medical guidance.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.169": "Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah occur in normalized English citations and are not duplicated in Urdu. The source's Bukhari 5371 is about a deceased debtor, not cupping; the relevant Bukhari 5696 names cupping and sea costus among the best treatments, so Urdu corrects both reference and the incomplete English gloss.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.176": "Bukhari and Muslim appear only in the retained normalized English citation. The source's supplement/heat/stasis interpretation is attributed to the author, not embedded in the hadith.",
    "ruqyah_details.text.195": "Bukhari appears only in the normalized English citation. Ibn Majah 3487 is graded weak by Darussalam on Sunnah.com; the source's Sahih label is not adopted as a verified grading."
